title: Hold on and plead (Berakhot 32a)
hookLine: Moses takes hold of God like a friend's sleeve, pleading for the people
tomorrow: if the gates of prayer can be locked, what's left?

cards: In a store, a small kid grabs a parent's sleeve and won't let go: please, please, please. Embarrassing, and completely sincere.
After the golden calf, God says to Moses in Exodus: "Now therefore let Me alone, that My wrath may wax hot against them." So what does Moses do? The Talmud says he does the opposite of letting go.

teach.b: Rabbi Abbahu says: if the verse weren't written, it would be impossible to say this.

Moses took hold of the Holy One like a person who grabs a friend by the garment, and said: Master of the world, I won't let You go until You forgive and pardon them. Look at the detail that sets it off.
Why would God say "let Me alone" unless someone was holding on? The rabbis hear the request as a door left open.

teach.h: FOR THE PEOPLE WHO MADE THE CALF.
teach.b: And look at who Moses is pleading for: the very people who just made the calf. Not himself. In Exodus, God relents.
So today's question: what does it look like to plead for someone? Here's a neighbor's story of pleading.

teach.h: SURAH HUD: ABRAHAM PLEADS FOR LOT'S PEOPLE.
teach.b: In the Qur'an, in Surah Hud, when Abraham hears the news the messengers bring, he begins to plead with God for the people of Lot, and the Qur'an praises him as gentle and quick to turn to God.
One honest difference: there, Abraham is told to leave it, because the decree has already come.
In the Talmud's story, Moses holds on and the people are spared. Both traditions honor the one who pleads for others; they tell differently what becomes of the plea.
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, God's "let Me alone" is read as an opening, and Moses uses it for people who'd just let him down.

how: Jews plead for others in prayer, for example in the Mi Shebeirach for the sick, often said in synagogue with the names of people who are ill.

games.q: what does “hold on and plead” mean?
o: refuse to let go while you plead for someone else
keep a grudge until someone asks you to forgive
hold tightly to your own side in an argument

games.q: who pleads for whom — tap the pairs.
p: pleads for the people of Lot

s: after the golden calf, Moses quietly accepted God's anger
the Talmud says he took hold like a friend at a garment and pleaded.
Rabbi Abbahu says the image would be impossible to say if the verse weren't written
were it not written, it couldn't be said.
in the Qur'an, Abraham pleads with God for the people of Lot
Surah Hud; he's praised, and told the decree has already come.

games.q: you're Jewish, your friend is Muslim, and a cousin you both love is in trouble. which idea from today could you both stand on?
o: pleading for someone else is honored in both traditions.
both traditions promise every plea will change the outcome.
neither tradition lets you plead for people who did wrong.
games.why: Moses pleads for the people of the calf; in Surah Hud, Abraham pleads for Lot's people and is praised. they differ on how the plea ends.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one person who's struggling right now. Hold their name the way Moses held on, not letting it slip away. If you pray, plead for them in your own words; if not, just keep them held in mind.

wordCard.voice: Hold on and plead. Moses grabs hold like a friend at a sleeve: I won't let You go until You forgive them.

orig.note: Hebrew, Exodus 32:10: let Me alone. the Talmud hears it as an opening for Moses to hold on.

carryVoice: Pocket line: hold on and plead, for someone else's sake. Twenty-four of fifty in Berakhot.

sources.q: Now therefore let Me alone, that My wrath may wax hot against them

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 32a (Rabbi Abbahu: Moses seized the Holy One like a man seizing his fellow by his garment)
Qur'an 11:74–76 (Surah Hud: Abraham pleads for the people of Lot; praised as forbearing and turning to God; told to leave it, for the command has come)
